is dialyzed on an Auto Analyzer. Reducing sugars are reacted .
with p-hydroxybenzoic acid hydrazide in a basic medium at
95°C and the absorbance is measured at 410 nm. Chlorogenic
acid is a positive interference. Standards are 1:1 glucose-
fructose. RSD‘at 29 for 2-30% reducing sugars is +6%. RSD
at 2¢ for 0,.2-2% reducing sugars is #11%.

There is an apparent concern within the Company for the
relatively low level of the tar-nicotine ratio in the smoke
produced by our products. Dr. Laurene discussed this
riefly in a meeting with the Research, Development and
Quality Control staffs on January 8, 1980. In discussing
the major points of emphasis for the 1980 R&D program, he
pointed out that we should approach a solution. to this con-
cern for relatively low tar-nicotine ratio levels in our
products by considering the tobaccos used in the formulation
of them.
Perhaps a brief review of the evolution in tobacco usage
for the production of cigarettes would clarify our present
position. At the time that five non-filtered products made
up approximately ninety percent of the domestic cigarette
sales, these products were formulated utilizing domestic
flue-cured, burley, and Maryland strips to make up approxi-
mately eighty-seven percent of the tobacco blend; oriental
tobacco made up approximately eight percent, and processed
stems about five percent. The casing and flavoring techno-
logy was relatively basic and uncomplicated when compared
to the technology that exists in the industry today. The
. technology in filters, filtration efficiencies, cigarette
Papers and dilution systems was essentially non-existant
and tar-nicotine ratio levels had not been conceived, The
domestic tobaccos were selected from farm erades produced
in the lower one-half to two-thirds of the plant. The
oriental leaf was selected from the "American Grades” pro-
duced in the upper part of the plant to achieve the rich-
ness and fullness of odor and taste imparted to the smoke
upon combustion.
The advent of the filtered cigarette and the increasing
acceptance of these products by the consumer have resulted x
. in €normous changes in the formulation of domestic Cigarettes. r=

May 10, 1978 |
Mr. A. P. Gaspar
Re: [FOCUS GROUPS FOR PROJECT "I" LO
Attached to this memo is the report on the focus groups for |
Project "I." My interpretation of the groups and the thoughts |
given in the report are in agreement. The groups were conducted |
in Cincinnati on April 12 and 13. :
:
Background
The focus groups were conducted to gain a qualitative reaction to
cigarette ideas directed at social problems connected with smoking,
The bulk of the discussion centered on four ideas:
1. A cigarette with no sidestream smoke.
2. A cigarette with 50% less sidestream smoke.
3. A cigarette with a pleasant aroma.
- 4. A cigarette which did not stain teeth or fingers.
Summary of Results
1. Smokers will not accept any modification in their cigarette
ne . which would adversely affect its taste. There seems to be a
. predisposition that any changes in a cigarette tend to adversely
affect the taste - perhaps a result of experience with low tar
cigarettes,
2. Smokers do feel that sidestream (or “raw") smoke can be bother-
some to both non-smokers and smokers due to the odor and irritation.
However, they did indicate that the smoke does have some
psychological benefits (the aroma, the visual pleasure of
watching the smoke, a feeling of comfort). Smokers were very
skeptical that a cigarette like this could deliver much taste.
3. A cigarette which gave off 50% (or noticeably) less smoke seemed
to be a reasonable compromise to many of the panel members. The
psychological benefits are retained, but there is less smoke to
collect in a house, gather on clothes, etc. However, most
members agreed that non-smokers would remain dissatisfied as
long as a cigarette gave off any smoke.

To: Dr. M, —. Stowe From: 0. €. Townsend
On January 24, John Mathews, Charles Mattina, and Dayid Burocher
from the Schweitzer Research Department gave a presentation to members of
Tobacco Davetogment ard Research. John Reynolds, Alan Moriman, and I
attended the meeting.
Mattina presented results which had been published earlier on the
influence of the cigarette wrapper on the smoke (Mattina & Selke, Proc.
ACS Symp., 173rd ACS Meeting - Agri & Food Chem Div, 1877). A comparison
was made of the permeability curves (flow vs aP) of inherently porous (IP)
and electrostatically perforated (£P) papers. While IP and EP papers may
have the same Coresta permeability (air fiow at 10 cm H,9 head), it was
shown that the EP papers at aP <1% cm HO permit greater air fiow and hence
should behave differently on a cigarette.
Free burn time decreases from about 12.5 to 7 minutes/40 mm with an
increase in Coresta permeability from about 5 to 100 cm/sec (constant blend
and citrate level).
The influence of paper burn additives on combustion with resnect to CO
production was discussed. Phosphate burn additive resulted in higher C0
deliveries than the citrate or untreated papers. While a number of prospective
burn additives fave been evaluated, none have heen found to result in CO
deliveries as low as those observed with untreated papers. Also it was
reported that on a per cigarette basis (0 deliveries pass through a maxtaum
with increasing citrate level. The maximum CO delivery occurs at about 0.8%
citrate, a value close to that used jn our commercial papers.
Mattina presented briefly the results of a Study of CO diffusion through
the wrapper of a cigarette. The results have been described tn detail previously
(Seitrage zur Tabak., 9 (4), 201 (1978)). In this study it was concluded that
there is little difference in the amount of CO diffusion from cigarettes
wrapped in papers of widely differing degrees of natural permeability.
John Mathews discussed the permeability range of commercial papers. He
stated that IP papers range from 6-200 cm/sec with 170-180 as a more practical
upper limit. Electrostatic papers range from 6-100 cm/sec in this country
with a substantially higher (180-200) upper limit in Europe.
Mathews discussed dilution air flow in vented filter tips as presented in
two earlier articles (Beitrage zur Tabak Int., 9 (4), 193 (1978} and o
Schweitzer Tech Bulletin, Mar. 15, 1977). In a comparison of mechanical and s
electrostatically perforated tipping (at constant total open hole area), it a
was found that electrically perforated tipping allowed 2-3 times greater air “
flow at ammweonstatit“plug wrap porosity. , $s

Re Minneapolis Metro Heavy Advertising Tes Results - Caniel
Background
Tn August 1993 a heavy advertising test was initiated for Camel in the Minneapolis metro
area. The purpose of the test was to assess whether heavier presence had an impact on
market sales. The test included fighted OOH, continuous print, and multiple visuals, and
the spending rate was al about double the national level
With the 1994 budget squeeze, national advertising spending was reduced as was
Minneapolis; however, the test area continued to receive support at about doubie the
national rate. Also in April 1994, the Camel BU began a heavy retail plan that
encompassed five regions and included Minneapolis
Methodology
We attempted to evaluate this test using traditional methods during 1993 (report issued
3/14/94 covering August-December 1993). Results from this early read indicated no
noticeable impact on sales. With Minneapolis becoming a retail heavy-up market in 1994
anda shifi in level of advertising support, this approach did not work for subsequent time
periods.
We approached IRT about doing a modeted technique, but based on their cost estimate of
$45,090 we clecied not to go with them. Instead, we utilized internal resources and Don
Schmidt in the BIAD Decision Support group developed the analytical approaches to
assess this issue.
Three analytical approaches were utilized: simple trend, forecasted baseline, and a
piodeled covariate procedure. The more sophisticated techniques provide a way to try to
separate out the effects of media from the other market effects that were going on at the
time, particularly pricing and promotion. All three approaches led to the same overall
conclusion,

Dear Dr. Mufson:
Thank vou for your expression of interest in our program of research support. Tam
Pleased to enclose a statement describing policies of The Council and a recent Annual Report
that lists grants currently supported. Our application procedure is a two step process. Firsi, a
short preliminary inquiry is sent to members of the Executive Committee of our Scientific
Advisory Board who evaluate it for scientific merit and for “fit” into The Council's current
multidisciplinary biomedical research program. If the Committee's review vote is positive,
you will be provided with Forms and instructions for completing a full application. In the
event you receive an award, The Council will consider up to nwo annual renewals on the basis
of progress reports and materials submitted with renewal applications.
The deadlines for submission of a full application are May 31 and November 30;
activation is typically seven months later. CTR accepts pircliminary applications continucusly— — ~
those received between April 1 and September 30 that are approved are eligible for the
November deadline; those received between October | and March 31 and are approved are
eligible For inclusion in the May cycle. The format for the preliminary application is as
Follows:
1, A three page narrative summary, This should contain a synopsis of the proposed project
including relevant background material, its present status and goals, a brief outline of the
research and its impact. The summary should end with a sentence indicating the
anticipated duration of the project (one, two or three years) and a single figure estimate of
the anticipated annual direct costs of the study as proposed. Please note thut the three
page limit is absolute; no attachment pages containing photographs, charts or literature
citations will be accepted. If you fudge such materials are critical for the review of the
proposal, they must be accomodated within tie tiree page limitation.
2. Two page curricula vitae and scientific bibliographies of the applicant and principal
professional level collaborators (the NIH format is quite acceptable), Again, the page limit
is strictly enforced, oniy two pages per investigator are forwarded to the Committee.
3. One copy cach of any two or three publications, abstracts or manuscripts that are closely
related to the project for which funding is being sought.

October 8, 1993
Gale A. Held, Director
State Prevention Systems Program
Center for Substance Abuse Prevention
Rockwall IE Building, 9th Floor
5600 Fishers Lane
Rockville, MD 20857
Dear Ms. Held:
As @ retail trade professional, | wish to object strenuously to the official harassment your
agency is proposing for my industry under the guise of enforcing Section 1926 of the
ADAMHA Reorganization Act,
The original language of Section 1926 is appropriate. Congress simply requires states
receiving ADAMHA block grants to enforce minimum age jaws for the purchase of tobacco
products in a manner “that can reasonably be expected to reduce” the availability of these
products to minors.
This language acknowledges that underage tobacco use. -- while a legitimate issue -- is not
in the same league as drug and alcohol abuse, the ovo evils ADAMHA funds are meant to
combat. It also assumes, rightly, that both the states and retailers are already committed
to enforcing and obeying all minimum age laws for the purchase of tobacco products.
The onerous and combative enforcement language proposed by HHS, by contrast, assumes
an adversarial relationship with retailers and imposes upon both the states and the retail
trade excessive costs and bureaucracy.
Rules proposed by FEHS would require retailers to bear an estimated $100 million annually
in compliance costs, HHS further suggests retailers absorb an additional $50 million a year
in law-enforcement costs through new licensing requirements.
Most distressing, HHS would subject retailers to the vigilante zeal of anti-smoking activists
by encouraging “private enuties" and “local governments” to employ children in conducting
frequent “sting” operations against unwary retailers.
Even more offensive, HHS suggests publishing the names of local stores entrapped in such
operations that “consumers who would wish to steer their patronage to stores which do not
violate the law” can do so. Please delete these provisions from the proposed rules.
In sum, the fantastic and excessive rules proposed by FEHS to measure compliance with
Section 1926 are unnecessary. Existing state laws, in conjunction with responsibte industry
programs promoung compliance with those laws, are more than sufficient.
Sineerely,
